deep.reconstruction:
PART 1. Rounding to the nearest Eisenstein integer ("Noch einfacher so" improves the three-case rule on the previous page). Let ε = e^{2πi/3}, so 1+ε+ε² = 0. A complex number m = a + bε + cε² is given with real (rational) a, b, c. Here [x] is the floor function.

The triple (a,b,c) is fixed only up to adding a common constant, since (a-s) + (b-s)ε + (c-s)ε² = m for every s.

Gauss's rule:
- Sort the fractional parts a-[a], b-[b], c-[c] as p ≤ q ≤ r.
- If p = q = r, subtract the common fractional part. This gives integer coefficients, so m is an Eisenstein integer.
- Otherwise there are three cyclic gaps on the circle R/Z: q-p, r-q and 1+p-r (their sum is 1). Take any t strictly inside the largest gap, i.e. in (p,q), (q,r) or (r,1+p) respectively.
- Then [a-t] + [b-t]ε + [c-t]ε² is the nearest Eisenstein integer.

Justification (mine):
- For real u, v, w, N(u+vε+wε²) = u²+v²+w²-uv-vw-wu = ½[(u-v)²+(v-w)²+(w-u)²].
- So we want integers A, B, C making the residuals a-A, b-B, c-C as tightly bunched as possible. Each residual is fixed mod 1.
- With A = [a-t] etc., every residual lies in [t, t+1). The residuals are the three fractional points lifted by cutting the circle at the chosen gap.
- Let the gaps be g1, g2, g3 and cut at g3. The pairwise residual differences are g1, g2, g1+g2, so the remainder has norm g1²+g1g2+g2².
- This matches the remainder norm ββ+βγ+γγ on the previous page.
- Compare cutting at g3 with cutting at g1: (g1²+g1g2+g2²) - (g2²+g2g3+g3²) = (g1-g3)(g1+g2+g3) = g1-g3.
- Hence the best cut is at the largest gap.
- Lifts that do not cut at a gap spread the residuals over more than 1 and are worse.
- The worst case is g1 = g2 = g3 = 1/3, giving remainder norm 1/3 < 1. This yields the Euclidean algorithm in Z[ε].

PART 2. Cyclotomic integers: computing the root r ≡ ε from the cofactor.
- ε is a primitive n-th root of unity (n prime, implicitly).
- fε = a + bε + cε² + ... is an integer of Z[ε], and m = N(fε) = ∏_{k=1}^{n-1} f(ε^k) is its 'Determinans'.
- The cofactor is Fε = m/fε = ∏_{k=2}^{n-1} f(ε^k) = A + Bε + Cε² + ..., an integer of Z[ε]. Write it as a polynomial F(x) with n coefficients A, B, C, ... (degree ≤ n-1).
- To fε corresponds a root r of x^n ≡ 1 (mod m), i.e. ε ≡ r mod fε. For fε a prime of degree 1, m = p ≡ 1 mod n.

Step 1, discrete Fourier inversion: n·(coefficient of x^j in F) = Σ_{k=0}^{n-1} ε^{-jk} F(ε^k). This gives the displayed lines:
- nA = F1 + Fε + Fε² + ...
- nB = F1 + ε^{-1}Fε + ε^{-2}Fε² + ...
- nC = F1 + ε^{-2}Fε + ε^{-4}Fε² + ...
- and so on.

Step 2: for j = 2, ..., n-1, F(ε^j) = σ_j(Fε) = ∏_{k≠1} f(ε^{jk}) contains the factor f(ε), because jk ≡ 1 for some k ≠ 1. So F(ε^j) ≡ 0 mod fε.

Step 3: modulo fε,
- nA - F1 ≡ Fε, nB - F1 ≡ ε^{-1}Fε, nC - F1 ≡ ε^{-2}Fε, nD - F1 ≡ ε^{-3}Fε.
- Hence nA - F1 - ε^k(n·coef_k - F1) ≡ 0 for each k. These are Gauss's three displayed congruences 'alle durch fε theilbar'.

Step 4: from nA - F1 ≡ ε(nB - F1) and nB - F1 ≡ ε(nC - F1), subtraction gives n(A-B) ≡ εn(B-C) mod fε.

Step 5: n = unit·(1-ε)^{n-1}, and fε is not divisible by the prime 1-ε. So n can be cancelled: A - B ≡ ε(B - C).

Step 6: ε ≡ (A-B)/(B-C) ≡ (B-C)/(C-D) ≡ (C-D)/(D-E) ≡ ... mod fε. Thus the root r of x^n ≡ 1 mod m belonging to the prime fε is read off from the cofactor's coefficients.

Equivalent formulation (mine): G(x) = (1-x)F(x) mod (x^n-1) vanishes at x = 1 and at x = r^j (j ≥ 2). So G ≡ c(x^n-1)/(x-r) mod p, whose coefficients form a geometric progression with ratio r. Using successive differences also removes the ambiguity F ↦ F + const·(1+x+...+x^{n-1}).
errors: Part 2: the divisibility of F(ε²), F(ε³), ... by fε holds unconditionally, because F(ε^j) contains the factor f(ε) for j ≠ 1. Gauss's hypothesis that fε, fε², ... be mutually coprime is not needed for that step. It is needed elsewhere: for the correspondence with a single root r and for B-C to be invertible mod fε.

Part 2, unstated (my fill): division by B-C needs B-C ≢ 0 mod fε. For fε a degree-1 prime with coprime conjugates this holds. If all successive differences vanished mod p, then Fε ≡ A(1+ε+...+ε^{n-1}) ≡ 0 mod p, so fε | Fε, contradicting coprimality.
Part 2: the inversion formulas require F written with n coefficients (degree ≤ n-1), including F(1) = A+B+C+... in the sums. Gauss's notation is consistent with this, though not stated.

Part 1: t must lie strictly inside the gap (Gauss's 'zwischen'). If two fractional parts coincide, one gap is 0, which is harmless. The rule presupposes a, b, c real, whereas on the previous page a, b, c meant the coefficients of the given m; consistent.

results.what: Nearest Eisenstein integer to a+bε+cε²: sort the fractional parts, cut the circle at the largest cyclic gap, and take floors of a-t, b-t, c-t. Remainder norm g1²+g1g2+g2² ≤ 1/3, giving the Euclidean division algorithm in Z[ω].
results.modern_name: Euclidean algorithm in Z[ω] / closest-point (decoding) algorithm for the hexagonal lattice A2 ≅ A2* (special case of sorting-based A_n* nearest-point algorithms)
results.usually_credited_to: Euclidean property of Z[ω]: Eisenstein (1844), also in Gauss's Nachlass on cubic residues. Sorting-based closest-point algorithms for A_n/A_n*: Conway & Sloane (1982) and later McKilliam–Clarkson–Quinn (2008).

results.what: Discrete Fourier inversion recovering the coefficients of F from the values F(ε^k).
results.modern_name: Inverse discrete Fourier transform over the n-th roots of unity
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Lagrange, Gauss, Vandermonde era); Gauss used it routinely

results.what: For a degree-1 prime fε of Z[ζ_n] with norm p, the root r ≡ ζ mod fε equals (A-B)/(B-C) ≡ (B-C)/(C-D) ≡ ... mod p, where A, B, C, ... are the coefficients of the cofactor N(fε)/fε.
results.modern_name: Explicit determination of the prime-ideal/root-of-unity correspondence (Kummer's cyclotomic prime factors, (p, ζ - r)) from the cofactor
results.usually_credited_to: Framework: Kummer (1844–1847, theory of cyclotomic integers). This specific coefficient-ratio formula has no standard attribution.

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's unpublished work on Eisenstein integers and on 'complex numbers' built from roots of unity (norms as 'Determinans', units) is partly known from the Nachlass/Werke. The Euclidean algorithm for Z[ω] is also expected of him. Notable unpublished details: the elegant largest-gap rounding rule, a special case of a modern lattice-decoding algorithm. Also the Kummer-style correspondence between prime factors and roots of x^n ≡ 1 mod m, with an explicit ratio formula for r. These are interesting but elementary, and his engagement with the topic is not unknown.

checkable.asserts: Norm of u+vε+wε² (ε³=1) equals u²+v²+w²-uv-vw-wu, the quantity minimized by the rounding rule.
Cutting at gap g3 instead of g1 changes the remainder norm by g1-g3, so cutting at the largest gap is optimal.
Maximum remainder norm is 1/3 < 1 (Euclidean property of Z[ω]).
For n=5, fε=2+ε (norm 11), the cofactor Fε has coefficients A..E = 10,2,6,4,5.
Gauss's ratios (A-B)/(B-C) ≡ (B-C)/(C-D) ≡ ... all give r = 9 ≡ -2 mod 11, the root with ε ≡ r mod 2+ε.
r=9 is indeed a root of x^5 ≡ 1 (mod 11).
fε·Fε = m = 11 in Z[ζ5], confirming Fε = m/fε.
